speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, yesterday in answer to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) I stated that 1,000 c.f.s. diversion at Chicago would have some effect on the seaway project. maintopic: ST, LAWRENCE SEAWAY FURTHER STATEMENT ON POSSIBLE EFFECTS OF DIVERSION AT CHICAGO
speechtext: I included the power project.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: ST, LAWRENCE SEAWAY FURTHER STATEMENT ON POSSIBLE EFFECTS OF DIVERSION AT CHICAGO
speechtext: In case I may have created a misapprehension or left the house under a misunderstanding, I think I should state now that the additional diversion of 1,000 c.f.s. will have an adverse effect upon navigation in the great lakes, and so far as the St. Lawrence river is concerned, while it is true that it would have little adverse effect during a high water cycle, I am informed it would have a detrimental effect on downstream interests during a period of low water.

speechtext:
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement to the house in regard to the 1952-53 wheat pool. Briefly, the record of the 1952-53 pool is as follows:
Receipts from producers from August 1, 1952 to July 31,	1953 amounted to
533,016,978-9 bushels. The pool also received 103,208,409-5 bushels from the 1951-52 pool by transfer and 2,110,381-9 bushels were received from others than producers. The total volume of wheat received by the 1952-53 pool was therefore 638,335,770-3 bushels. The pool commenced with an initial payment of $1.40 per bushel basis No. 1 northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver. On March 2, 1953 the initial price was increased to $1.60 per bushel and an adjustment payment of 20 cents per bushel was made on all grades of wheat except Durums, delivered to the pool between August 1, 1952 and February 28, 1953. On September 24, 1953 an interim payment of 12 cents per bushel was authorized and paid on all grades of wheat delivered to the 1952-53 pool by producers.
Of these total receipts of 638,335,770-3 bushels, remaining stocks on January 30, 1954 were 148,679,561-7 bushels against which the board had priced open sales contracts of 21,404,291-1 bushels. The net stock position on January 30, 1954 was 127,275,270 -6 bushels.
The Canadian wheat board has recommended that the 1952-53 pool be closed as at January 30, 1954 and remaining stocks as well as priced open contracts be transferred to the 1953-54 pool as at January 30, 1954. The board further recommended that priced open contracts should be transferred

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Wheat
on the basis of contract prices and that unsold stocks of wheat should be transferred basis at market prices less an allowance for carrying charges subsequent to the transfer and for market risks.
The government has concurred in the wheat board's recommendation in respect to closing the 1952-53 pools and the basis of the transfer to the 1953-54 pool.
The final surplus in the 1952-53 pool is $58,282,438.38 after deducting the Prairie Farm Assistance Act levy and final payment expenses and adding estimated interest earnings subsequent to January 30, 1954. This is the net surplus payable to producers and amounts to an average of 10-934 cents per bushel on their deliveries to the 1952-53 pool.
I might add that including the proceeds of the interim payment last fall, which amounted to $63,962,036.83, the total surplus in the 1952-53 pool was $122,244,475.21 over and above the adjusted initial price of $1.60 per bushel basis No. 1 northern in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver. This compares with the final surplus in the 1951-52 pool of $114,585,112.69.
The final 1952-53 payment to producers on the principal grades of wheat will be as follows:	No. 1 northern, 9-653 cents per
bushel; No. 2 northern, 9-963 cents per bushel; No. 3 northern, 10-341 cents per bushel; No. 4 northern 13-454 cents per bushel; No. 5 wheat 9-292 cents per bushel; No. 6 wheat 14-397 cents per bushel; feed wheat, 14 -679 cents per bushel.
The foregoing payments also apply on toughs and damps of each grade.
Prior to the deduction of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act levy, the net price realized by producers for No. 1 northern wheat basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver will be $1-81871 per bushel. The corresponding realized price for the 1951-52 pool was $1-83569 per bushel.
The house will be interested in the results obtained in respect to milling grades of Durum wheat. During 1952-53 board receipts of Durum wheat were 8,288,289-8 bushels. Hon. members will recall that effective March 2, 1953, the initial price of Durum grades of wheat was increased to $1.65 per bushel basis No. 1 amber Durum and the adjustment payment on all grades of Durum was 25 cents per bushel. The high final payments on milling grades of Durum wheat are due to a very active demand for this variety of wheat and a limited supply not only in Canada but in other exporting countries.
The wheat board is in a position to commence the distribution of the final payment on the 1952-53 wheat pool on or about March 15.

subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST PUBLICATIONS IN CANADA SUBSIDIZED FROM ABROAD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. It is based on an article in today's Montreal Gazette, reporting a statement made by an official of the citizenship branch, to which I have called the minister's attention. My question is this. Does the government hold the view there expressed that there exists in Canada a group of communist publications whose aim is the furtherance in Canada of the objects of international communism, which are subsidized from abroad, guided from Toronto, and aimed chiefly at new Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST PUBLICATIONS IN CANADA SUBSIDIZED FROM ABROAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member indicated that he intended to ask a question but until I heard him speak just now I did not know what the question was going to be. I have seen the article referred to in the Montreal Gazette. It is a report, which is not in quotation marks, of a lecture delivered last evening to a group known as the Montreal co-ordinating council for new immigrants. In so far as the report is concerned I see in it nothing that is contrary to the knowledge that exists in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The citizenship branch particularly has in it liaison officers whose duty it is to visit groups of new Canadians, to see that they understand the perils of communism as it is preached in Canada, and to take active steps to prevent new immigrants from coming under the influence of these people. Parliament votes the money for that purpose, and I think that duty is being carried out reasonably well.
So far as concerns the opinion expressed that there is in Toronto a headquarters from which communist propaganda is disseminated, I think it is common knowledge that the headquarters of the Labour-Progressive party was at one time, if it is not now, in the city of Toronto. I think it is also common knowledge that there are 12 or 14 foreign language newspapers which follow the communist line. The speaker, Mr. Boyd, was attempting to show how they followed a common line in


almost everything, including an effort to undermine all the institutions in Canada that we try to uphold.

subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST PUBLICATIONS IN CANADA SUBSIDIZED FROM ABROAD
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration or possibly the Minister of Justice, or both. ^ I should like to ask whether there exists _ in Canada any legislation under which effective action can be taken to deal with this alleged communist-directed group who are aiming newspaper propaganda at new citizens. If so, I should like to ask what plan the government has for action accordingly?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST PUBLICATIONS IN CANADA SUBSIDIZED FROM ABROAD
speechtext: Is that question not in the nature of asking the minister to give a legal opinion?

subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST PUBLICATIONS IN CANADA SUBSIDIZED FROM ABROAD
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ALLEGED COMMUNIST PUBLICATIONS IN CANADA SUBSIDIZED FROM ABROAD

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a question similar to that one has been asked on a number of previous occasions; but if there is objection to the form of the question, perhaps I could put it this way. As to the legal position with regard to any action to be taken against persons, I think my hon. friend will know perfectly well that that matter rests with the attorneys general of the provinces to prefer prosecutions under any laws there may be on the subject and for offences under them.

speakerposition: stagedirection

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF COAL ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to address a question to the Minister of Transport. Can the minister inform the house the reasons

why the Canadian National Railways cancelled a coal order that was to be supplied by the Drummond colliery located at West-ville, Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANCELLATION OF COAL ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was courteous enough to send me notice of his question. I had been expecting this question now for some days and I had asked the Canadian National Railways for an explanation of the position. This is what the railways tell me.
The Intercolonial Coal Company ceased operations on October 29, 1953, after the mine was closed down. It was purchased by a Mr. Henry Thompson of New Glasgow and reopened as the Drummond Coal Company. The coal was never good but since the mine has reopened it has been even worse. There were delays in train service in December, January and early February due to the use of Drummond coal which was supplied to our locomotives at Joffre. On account of the complaints received from the operating department our fuel department has recently been sampling and analysing a number of cars of Drummond coal received at Joffre. The average ash content was 22-7 per cent which was about 3J per cent higher than that of the coal we previously received from the Intercolonial Coal Company. Additional impurities have been found in the coal in the form of a hard heavy stone which the railways understand is known locally in Westville as "iron stone". The samples of this material indicate that it is hard and large enough to cause serious trouble to stokers of our locomotives. Apart from a small tonnage, the C.N.R. are receiving no coal from any other source that approaches 19 per cent ash, and for the reasons given above the C.N.R. have refused to continue taking Drummond coal. The maximum ash content accepted on United States coal is 10 per cent and on Canadian coal it is 14 per cent.
That is the purport of the information given to me by the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 297, to amend the Bank of Canada Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned on the first reading of this bill, many of the proposed amendments to the Bank of Canada Act deal with rather minor matters and to a considerable extent involve a tidying up of the act. Since it is the intention that this bill be sent to the banking and commerce committee as soon as it has received second reading, it does not seem to me necessary or desirable that I should go into these matters of detail in the house at this stage. However, with respect to the more important amendments which are being proposed, members 83276-155
Bank of Canada Act
might find it of some help if I gave a brief review of the considerations underlying the changes involved.
Perhaps I might start by reviewing the present and proposed provisions regarding the chartered banks' cash reserves. At the present time the chartered banks are required to maintain at all times a cash reserve equal to at least 5 per cent of their Canadian dollar deposit liabilities. This requirement was established in 1934 following a period in which the cash reserves of individual banks had on occasion fallen to rather low levels.
I might say that now, with a central bank in operation, it is inconceivable that a situation would arise where there would be a shortage of cash reserves such as existed in the early 1930's.
Minimum cash reserve requirements are important not only because they ensure that banks will maintain an adequate liquid position but also because of their relationship to the cash reserve policy of the central bank. The most important function of the Bank of Canada is to influence the volume of money and credit, and the normal way in which this influence is brought to bear is through changes in the cash reserves of the banks. An increase in cash reserves tends to encourage banks to expand their assets; a decrease tends to discourage expansion. However, the effectiveness of the cash reserve policy depends to a considerable extent on the firmness of the relationship between the banks' cash reserves and deposit liabilities. If the banks allow the relationship to vary much, there may be no response, or only a very slow response, to a change in cash reserves. The minimum cash reserve requirement is important in this connection since it establishes a level at which banks must respond to decreases in their cash reserves.
Experience has shown that the 5 per cent minimum is too far below the ratio which each bank normally regards as its target-in the neighbourhood of 10 per cent-to prevent the banks in certain circumstances from allowing, even though reluctantly, their average cash ratio to fall well below the target level. In an inflationary period, when demands for bank loans are at a peak, and when it is appropriate for the central bank to attempt to restrain the expansion of money and credit, banks are sometimes willing to allow their average cash ratios to fall below the normal target level and the size of the central bank's task becomes very much greater. In such a situation the present methods of central bank action available to the Bank of Canada may not always be sufficient to cope with the problem of restraining credit expansion in an effective

Bank of Canada Act
and orderly way. This is also true of situations where other special factors, such as the inflow of foreign funds, may create a temporary but substantial excess of cash reserves.
To overcome these difficulties it is proposed that the minimum cash reserve requirement, based on the daily average for each calendar month, be 8 per cent of deposit liabilities and that the Bank of Canada be given power to vary this minimum requirement between 8 and 12 per cent, provided that the chartered banks are given a minimum period of one month's notice before each increase becomes effective and that any one increase is not more than 1 per cent. When this legislation comes into force, the initial minimum requirement will of course be 8 per cent. Having in mind that the 8 per cent minimum will be calculated on a daily average basis, I do not feel that the practical result will involve a more onerous requirement than the present arrangement.
The addition of the power to vary reserve requirements to the techniques now available to the Bank of Canada in implementing monetary policy will bring them into line with those of central banks in other countries. However, it is not the intention or expectation that this power is one which will be frequently used. Much more likely it will be limited to special and temporary situations where the present methods of restraining monetary expansion need to be supplemented. Incidentally, it is believed that an announcement by the central bank of an increase in reserve requirements would have helpful psychological effects. It would be a specific indication to the chartered banks' customers that restraint in the use of credit was necessary, and that the banks' capacity to increase loans was being restricted.
Until now, the requirement that banks observe a minimum cash reserve requirement has appeared in both the Bank of Canada Act and the Bank Act. It is now proposed that only the provisions regarding the power to vary the requirement should be included in the Bank of Canada Act. All other provisions relating to cash reserve requirements, including the detailed provisions with respect to the basis on which the requirement is to be observed and the statistical information and declarations which are to be maintained, will be made part of the Bank Act and will be available for discussion when the amending legislation is introduced.
In addition to the amendment regarding cash reserve requirements, there are three

other important proposed revisions which I might mention briefly. In view of the proposed provision in the National Housing Act allowing banks to make insured mortgage loans, it is proposed that the Bank of Canada should have the power to make short-term loans to banks on the pledge or hypothecation of mortgages held by them.
At the present time there are certain limitations on the amount of securities, issued or guaranteed by the government of Canada or any province, which the Bank of Canada is allowed to hold. Holdings of such securities which do not mature within two years are limited to 50 per cent of the bank's outstanding note issue and deposit liabilities, and holdings of securities which do not mature within ten years are limited to an amount equal to five times the paid-up capital and rest fund of the bank. It is felt that these arbitrary limitations are no longer necessary or desirable and it is proposed to remove them. At the same time it is proposed that greater detail of the bank's securities holdings be given in the weekly and monthly returns to the Minister of Finance which are published in the Canada Gazette.
The rest fund of the bank is now just over $10 million, having been provided out of profits in accordance with the original act. Owing to the substantial growth of the total assets of the bank, it is thought that additional capital funds should be provided by increasing the rest fund to $25 million. This would be accomplished by appropriating one-fifth of the annual profits to the rest fund each year until the desired level is reached.
As I indicated at the outset of my statement, Mr. Speaker, I propose, at the conclusion of the debate on second reading, to move that the bill be referred to the banking and commerce committee, and the governor of the Bank of Canada will be available to explain the technical aspects of the amendments which are being made to the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MANAGEMENT, EXCHANGE, TO PERMIT SHORT TERM LOANS ON INSURED MORTGAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
As the
minister has indicated, this measure will go to the banking and commerce committee, so it is neither desirable nor possible at the moment to talk about the details. It seems to me that the measure is of great importance in extending the powers of the Bank of Canada, and it seems to me also it is worthwhile to dwell just for a few moments on the vast powers which the Bank of Canada has, and has had over the last 20 years. We have come to take them so much for granted that we do not often think about them. I propose to spend a very short time in directing attention to them.

As the minister has indicated, apart from details of personnel of directors and their remuneration, the three things that this measure really does are, first, to introduce a new power with regard to mortgages and real estate; secondly, to extend to some extent the general investment powers of the bank, though that is not very far-reaching; and thirdly, to deal with the question of chartered banks' reserves and their relationship to the Bank of Canada.
I said a moment ago I though it was worthwhile to draw attention to the really vast powers over our day to day lives that have been vested in the Bank of Canada. I think these powers could best be indicated by reading the preamble to the act, but even before that I should read a short extract from the Macmillan report outlining what that commission considered to be the duties of a central bank.
I hope you are not getting uneasy, Mr. Speaker, because it does seem to me-I assure you I shall be brief-that when we are extending substantially the powers of this institution, as we are, it is relevant to spend a very few moments in reminding ourselves, as we very seldom do, of the very great powers that institution has. I submit that with deference, Mr. Speaker, and also with a good deal of earnestness. The Macmillan report says briefly at page 63:
. . . the central bank . . . should endeavour to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation and should so far as possible control and defend the external value of the national monetary unit. In the second place, from the international point of view, the central bank by wise and timely co-operation with similar institutions in other countries, should seek, so far as may lie within the scope of monetary action, to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of economic activity.
I now wish to read the preamble to the Bank of Canada Act, because it really echoes some of the words of the Macmillan report. The preamble is short and says:
Whereas it is desirable to establish a central bank in Canada to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action, and generally to promote the economic and financial welfare . . . etc.
I just wish, Mr. Speaker, to say a further word about the extreme range of those powers-to regulate credit and currency, to control and protect the external value of the monetary unit. It is no exaggeration to say that the action of the Bank of Canada affects every one of us in our lives because, to go no farther, here you have a power placed 83276-155i
Bank of Canada Act
in the hands of a few men who are in close conjunction with the government. These few men have the power of controlling the spendable money in circulation in Canada. I need not point out what that means to all of us. It means that the central bank, by its actions, can stimulate or slow down the economic activity of the country. It can have a great influence on prices, and I need not explain why. The argument is perfectly obvious.
Then the central bank has great power over the chartered banks. We have discussed that in the house before. It is no exaggeration to say that the chartered banks really need nothing but a request from the central bank in order to comply with that request.
At any rate, I think that is a fair summary of what has happened in the last 20 years, and particularly the last 15 years, during which time the central bank has played a very important part in our lives. I am referring of course to the 15 years since the outbreak of war.
That would lead one to ask this question: is there any restriction of any kind on the powers of the central bank, or is it left to the judgment of a group of men to exercise this important function?

speechtext:
I defer to Your Honour's ruling, of course; perhaps unintentionally I may have wandered. However, I think Your Honour will agree that the point I am now going to make is entirely relevant, because it has to do with the question of whether there should be any restriction of power in any way. And I suggest to Your Honour that the real principle of the measure before us is that it does extend very substantially the powers of the Bank of Canada.
I am now about to refer-this is really my last point, and I can reassure Your Honour as to the question of the time during which I shall speak-to a restriction of the bank's power which, I suggest, is relevant because in the measure the government seeks actually to make the powers still wider.
The point I wish to raise now, one which I am sure Your Honour will find is well within the limits of the rules, is that I now ask the question whether there is at the present time any restriction-and I can answer that there is not, and that the Bank of Canada at the present time really has no restrictions over its powers of creating currency. But I would point out that when the bank was set up there was such a restriction, which has now been done away with. It is the doing away with that restriction to which I wish to refer, and in that connection to quote some of the experts who have expressed opinions in the matter.
I repeat that when we are extending powers, as we are in this measure, surely it is relevant to consider whether the powers are unlimited, whether they were always unlimited, and the reason for the removal of the limitations. We must consider whether there is an argument to be made for the restoration of some limitation.
In this connection I should like to read section 23, formerly section 26, of the Bank of Canada Act which says:
(1)	The bank shall always maintain a reserve, as hereinafter provided, as security against its outstanding notes and deposit liabilities.
(2)	The reserve required by this section to be maintained shall consist of gold coin and bullion in the unrestricted ownership of the bank equal to an amount not less than 25 per cent of the notes and deposit liabilities aforesaid.
That restriction, I am informed, was removed in 1940, during the war, and all the gold that was in the custody of the bank was then transferred to the management of the foreign exchange control board for the foreign exchange fund. And from that time


until 1952 an order in council was passed, year by year, rendering the maintenance of the reserve unnecessary.
Then in 1952 the following section was passed in the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act:
Notwithstanding section 26-
And that is now section 23.
-of the Bank of Canada Act, the Bank of Canada is not, unless the governor in council otherwise prescribes, required to maintain a minimum or fixed reserve ratio of gold or foreign exchange to its liabilities.
In other words, Your Honour, we now have a situation wherein the brake which did exist has been entirely removed.
I should like in that connection to refer to an extract from the Macmillan report, which was the basis of the setting up of the bank. I refer particularly to a statement made by Sir Thomas White who, at one time, occupied the position now occupied by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). Sir Thomas White has very strong words to say about the maintenance of a 25 per cent gold reserve. It will be noted that Sir Thomas White and Mr. Leman of Montreal, who was at that time the general manager of one of the banks, filed dissenting memoranda. Sir Thomas White said:
I join with my colleague, Mr. Leman, in his strong criticism of granting to the board of the proposed bank the power to carry their cash reserves either in gold or foreign exchange. He has pointed out the grave risk involved in relying to too great an extent upon the stability of such exchange and to the necessity for maintaining a 25 per cent gold reserve in Canada.
I mention that merely to show that that view was held by competent people at that time. And as I have mentioned Sir Thomas White I should like to add that some of the views he held which some people were inclined to regard as old-fashioned eight or nine years ago, have now proved to be not so old-fashioned, at a time when Dominion of Canada bonds are selling on a 3-75 basis.
In the committee on the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act of two years ago we had a very interesting sitting attended by the late Dr. Clark, then deputy minister. I should like to read briefly from one or two of the answers he gave, because I think they are relevant. Dr. Clark answered a question I had asked him-and which purposely I had put in a rather extreme form-in this way:
Perhaps I should ask you now whether you accept fully the view that after all we have a managed currency and there is no check of any kind on it except the judgment of a group of men of whose judgment we think highly and if that is a fair statement of your attitude does that mean that you feel that we should entirely dismiss from our minds the idea of reserve, that we have outgrown them?

To that he answered, "no, no." Mr. Dumas also asked Dr. Clark:
Would you say that it would be in the interest of the country, if in our reserve we had more gold than we have, if we had gold instead of U.S. dollars.
To that Dr. Clark answered:
I do not think it makes very much difference. There are reasons for which you want gold and there are reasons for which you want U.S. dollars. We keep a certain amount in both . . . the amount we are holding in gold has been increasing recently.
I want now to apologize here for quoting briefly from my own remarks when speaking two years ago in the committee of the whole in the debate on the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act. I was pleased to find this because I am glad to know that I am not talking differently today from the way I talked two years ago. That is always a satisfaction to anyone in our way of life. I should like to quote from page 3786 of Hansard of June 26, 1952, where I am reported as follows:
In the discussion in the banking and commerce committee yesterday this point of a fixed reserve was raised, and I should like to put this discussion briefly on the record.
Let me say here, lest I forget, that I am not suggesting that Dr. Clark had committed himself to the 25 per cent gold reserve. I am suggesting merely that he did not sweep out the idea of a reserve as something which sensible men could not talk about.
There is of course the view which has been expressed in this house this afternoon that money should be entirely a managed thing, that there should be no attempt to impose a check of any kind.
I want to interject here to say that it will be remembered that in 1947 there were strong differences of opinion among us as to the parity at which the Canadian dollar had been fixed and there was a great loss at that time of gold and American exchange. I think anyone, whether he agrees or not with the desirability of having a gold reserve, will agree that if there had been a provision for a gold reserve we would at that time have had to stop, look and listen earlier, and to some of us that would have been an advantage.
That was discussed in the committee yesterday, and I think it would be fair to say the view of the experts was that while at the present time they felt that it was wise to leave in abeyance clause 26-
Now clause 23.
-of the Bank of Canada Act-in other words they did not think it was wise to reimpose the requirement of 25 per cent gold backing of the currency- nevertheless they did not go the length of saying that a reserve check of some kind was an outmoded superstition.
And then later on I said:
I am not going to pursue this at length, but I do want to have it on the record that I think the question of a reserve of some kind, a check on the
Bank of Canada Act
purely managed currency, should not be regarded as an outworn superstition. I think it should be seriously considered. I am not going to ask the committee to spend time considering it this afternoon. I am anxious just to put it on the record.
Incidentally, when we come to the committee I hope that that will be considered seriously. We are in danger I think of having almost too much satisfaction in our supreme wisdom and forgetting that there are events beyond our control. We have in fact been going through 15 years of boom and that does not always give one all the answers.
I want to thank you, sir, for your kindness in allowing me to put forward these views and I on my part intend to co-operate with you by carrying out what I said about not speaking at length. I do hope that when we get to committee this matter will be taken seriously. I think we should remember that, as I said at the outset, we have under this act put in the power of a few men almost unbelievable control over the lives of the rest of us.
As I have said, for 15 years we have been in a boom and we are inclined to think that that was due to our supreme wisdom. It has been due very largely to events over which we have no control. Therefore I hope that when we come to the committee we shall be ready with open minds to consider the situation and I hope that the chairman of the committee will be as indulgent as you have been and permit a discussion again of metallic reserves.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MANAGEMENT, EXCHANGE, TO PERMIT SHORT TERM LOANS ON INSURED MORTGAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, as has already been said by the minister and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), will go to the banking and commerce committee. I am sure that we all hope that in the banking and commerce committee there will be a very thorough review of the Bank of Canada Act and that the proposals contained in this bill will be thoroughly considered and discussed.
I may say that in a general way we are in support of this bill. There are details which our members on the committee will inquire into, question and perhaps make some further proposals. I think time has vindicated the establishment of the Bank of Canada.
Perhaps it may not be out of place if I paid a tribute to the people who pioneered the idea very largely in this house, and indeed across the country. An examination of Hansard in the period from 1921 to 1935 will, I think, indicate very clearly who they were. Mainly they were the members of a very able group of farmers and labour men who occupied the southeast corner of this chamber. It was a strange turn of events

Bank of Canada Act
in 1935 that saw most of them eliminated from this house. I think the educational work which they did was used and that the monetary proposals they made were brought to an illogical conclusion, mainly in the province of Alberta in 1934 and 1935.
This bank was established first by the government of the late Viscount Bennett, partly as a publicly-owned and partly as a privately-owned institution. In 1936 it was thought proper that it should be brought under public control and made entirely a publicly-owned institution. As this bill very clearly indicates, the bank was established to serve a number of purposes. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Greenwood, its primary function then was and still is "to control or regulate the volume of credit and money in circulation".
Prior to that time the legislation pertaining to the issue of notes, paper currency, money and so on, was unsatisfactory. Then again central banks were being created throughout the commonwealth. We therefore created this institution. We are now called upon to consider and amend the act under which it was created. In the years before there was very little control over bank policies by the parliament of Canada or by any institution reporting to the parliament of Canada.
The chartered banks had the privilege of extending credit and issuing their own bank notes. The only control was within the institutions themselves, within the chartered banks. Mainly they thought in terms of the safety of their depositors' money. I readily recognize that, although there was the added incentive of protecting their own institutions and of profit to their shareholders.
The factors which brought about this act, factors which are still with us and therefore would come under a discussion of the amendments, are dangers inherent in any banking system. The general public became anxious about the safety of their deposits. This was brought home to them at the time of the failure of the Home Bank and the difficulties into which the Merchants Bank got in the 1920's. Then of course there was the financially dangerous situation which developed in the early thirties when the government of that day found it necessary, in order to prevent panic, to allow the banks to publish balance sheets showing their securities at the figures of a few years earlier, when the assets were greatly inflated.
I say this because when this bill comes before the banking and commerce committee and amendments are considered I think these

facts should be borne in mind. Another factor, of course, which promoted the original bill was the fact that under a competitive commercial banking system there should be a central bank to control currency and credit. That was evident in the twenties and thirties when credit was extended in boom times, and called in when depression came. I think a cursory reading of the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, in 1933, will confirm that this was so.
The purpose of this bill, I take it, is to do what we have actually been doing over the last 20 years or more, namely to define more clearly the powers and function of this institution in the light of experience. No one seeks to change that complete monopoly over the issue of all forms of currency, but under the Bank Act of 1934 it was contemplated that the banks would continue to issue some currency. However, in 1944 it was decided that that privilege would cease immediately, and in 1950 any outstanding notes issued by the chartered banks were taken over by the Bank of Canada and the banks paid the Bank of Canada the value of those remaining in circulation at that time.
As the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) said, these amendments do not interfere in any respect with the monopoly given to the Bank of Canada in these matters, nor does it in any way interfere with their responsibilities in carrying out their functions in accordance with the act. Consequently, the issue of credit and particularly currency today is, of course, not only the responsibility of the Bank of Canada but, indeed, the responsibility of this parliament, whose instrument the Bank of Canada is.
The minister is now suggesting that the legal reserves which must be carried with the Bank of Canada by the chartered banks shall be increased from 5 to 8 per cent, and under certain circumstances up to 12 per cent. I believe that was the figure the minister gave. That is an increased safety factor.
As a matter of fact, I believe the banks themselves in the last few years have not maintained a reserve of 5 per cent, but have maintained reserves considerably in excess of that figure extending at times to the higher figure which the minister mentioned in the course of his remarks. Hence, from now on, the banks will have rather less discretion than they had before as to the ratio of cash reserves to their liabilities to their depositors. I believe this will be satisfactory to the people of Canada who will feel that this is a more adequate protection or will be when these amendments are written into the Bank of Canada Act.

Of course, this ratio which the minister proposes is an important factor in the regulation or control of the credit the banks may issue to the public. Our central bank through its operations can expand or contract the country's credit simply by increasing or decreasing the reserves of the chartered banks, and to my mind, though this may not be the most important, it is a most important function of the Bank of Canada.
I believe that was demonstrated in the early years of the depression in another country, and I remember when this act was under discussion trying to bring to the attention of the house the operations carried on in Sweden, where they used the open market and where, when they needed to put money into circulation, they bought government securities. When they wanted to take money out of circulation they sold government securities with the result that in the early 1930's, when we had financial and grave economic difficulties, Sweden was in a fairly happy position. They were able to bring about a certain amount of stability in their economic relations and in their financial system through open market operations. Now the Bank of Canada can reduce the cash reserves of the banks by selling some of its large holdings of government securities. Conversely it can buy securities and thus increase the amount of credit available for loans.
I believe that, because of the provision in the bill for an increase of legal cash reserves, we are protected to an extent that we were not protected in the early years of the 1930's or in any other period of boom which came before the depression of the 1930's. When the central bank has paid for securities by means of a cheque drawn on the chartered bank concerned, and when this cheque is presented for payment at the chartered bank, it results in the reduction of its reserve deposits with the Bank of Canada and therefore limits the amount of credit it may grant. Conversely, if they wish to adopt the other course they can expand credit to an extent.
The late Dr. Clark, whom the hon. member for Greenwood quoted a few moments ago, gave another very interesting slant to the Bank of Canada Act which I would like to draw to the attention of the house, because these amendments emphasize Dr. Clark's opinions. Speaking before the banking and commerce committee of 1944 when the last decennial review of the chartered banks' charters and the Bank of Canada Act were under discussion, Dr. Clark said:
The Bank of Canada is the channel through which the monetary policy of the government is put into effect.
Bank of Canada Act
In other words, Dr. Clark believed that in reviewing the charters and the Bank of Canada Act we were not only reviewing the policies of the banks and of the central bank but were also reviewing the financial policy of the government, because it is the financial policy of the government which is carried out by the central bank.
It seems then that this institution is not by itself responsible for the policies which it puts into effect, for it puts into effect the policies approved by the government. Consequently, the government must take responsibility for the success or failure of policies which are put into effect through the central bank.
May I also add that I hope the committee will make a pretty thorough review of what these policies have been in recent years. I believe that that can be done, because the bill contains wide powers and considerable latitude. For example, the bank may buy and sell bullion from the United States. It may also buy and sell:
. . . short term securities issued by the United Kingdom . . . having a maturity not exceeding six months from the date of acquisition by the bank;
There is an indication of government policy, a policy which lays it down that certain securities of the United States may be bought without limitation as to the period, but that the United Kingdom securities may be bought provided that they have a maturity not exceeding six months from the date of acquisition by the bank. I think that that is a matter into which the committee should inquire very carefully, namely, as to why this provision is in the bill. It has puzzled me and I have no doubt that the committee will try to elucidate it.
I think that we should also inquire into the effect of the government's policies regarding currency and credit upon the economy and the people of Canada over the last number of years. In looking over the reports of the Bank of Canada I have been struck with the fact that the money supply in Canada has largely outrun or gone beyond the gross national production. Why was that the policy of the government since the war? Was it that another policy might have interfered with the value of government securities in Canada such as bonds and so on? I do not know. However, I think that matter should be looked into very carefully.
I think also that when the committee considers these amendments, they might consider how the efficiency of the control of currency and credit can be improved. Of course, at the moment, you have the central

Bank of Canada Act
bank and you have the chartered banks and at times there is to some extent a conflict of interest between them. The chartered banks are profit-making institutions naturally and their interests do not always lie along the same road as that of the policy which the Bank of Canada is carrying out. It seems to me that when you have an increase in the money supply at a time when the production of goods is not keeping pace with that increase, you are bound to have inflation. I would ask the committee to go into the situation with a view to seeing what effect the policies of the bank and the banking institutions have had in the last seven or eight years on inflation in Canada.
I do not want to go beyond the scope of this bill. I had perhaps intended to do so but when Mr. Speaker suggested to my friend the hon. member for Greenwood that he should not do so and my hon. friend agreed, I felt that I would try to do the same thing. However, I should like to point this out. In 1945 the gross national production in dollars of constant value-and I am using as a dollar of constant value the dollar in its purchasing power between 1935 and 1939- was $9,315 million; in 1950 it was $10,330 million, again using what I have termed "dollars of constant value". In 1945, our total money supply was $5,905 million. In 1950 it had risen to $8,712 million. That is a rise of approximately $1,000 million in gross national production compared with a rise of approximately $2,800 million in the money supply. By "money supply" I mean the public's deposits with the banks, ignoring Canada savings bonds, short-term government securities or other savings of the public that are found in other financial institutions.
As I say, such figures raise in my mind at least an immediate question. Is the central bank of Canada, with its present powers under this act, and with the amendments that we are proposing to make in this bill, able to control the supply of money to the extent necessary to combat inflation or-what is equally important-to prevent deflation? We may be entering upon a time when deflation may be as significant to us as inflation has been over the last few years.
Of course we believe that other powers are required than those which are contained in the act or in the proposed amendments to the act. As is generally known, we favour the public ownership and control of the commercial banks because we believe that eventually that course will be necessary. We also point out the desirability of controlling the flow of investments, a matter which I will not discuss this afternoon. We think
[Mr. Coldwell.1
that a national investment board to direct investments into socially desirable channels is a step which should be taken. We set up an industrial development bank. I do not know just how successful it has been and I am not going to discuss that matter now. But we believe that there exists a gap which should be filled. May I say to my friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that it is not a new idea to him because it was in the Liberal election platform during more than one election campaign some years ago.

speechtext:
What I am getting at is this. I do not think that the government has used all the powers given in the Bank of Canada Act. Perhaps in seeking the new powers it has in mind doing something more. However, it has not used the powers it has to control credit to the extent which under the act- I mean under the main act-would have helped to prevent the post-war inflation that we have suffered. Indeed, it was not until 1951 that the governor of the Bank of Canada met the managements of the chartered banks, and came to an agreement with them that certain changes would be made, and that action was taken after the inflationary damage had very largely been done.
If I may, I should like to quote from a document in support of what I have just said, namely an article entitled "Recent Developments in Canadian Monetary Policy" published in the American Economic Review last May, at page 55. The author is Mabel F. Timlin of the University of Saskatchewan. The quotation is as follows:
In only one year shown in the annual reports of the bank (namely 1947) did the record show a decline in chartered bank reserves and the governor has explained (annual report of the Bank of Canada, 1947, pages 23 to 24) that the correlative decline in security holdings of the central bank was a consequence of government redemptions at a time when the bank was otherwise an active purchaser of short and medium-term bonds. The total series of reports (i.e. annual reports covering the bank's entire history) shows a reserve expansion of nearly $670 million and the astonishing thing is that 31 per cent, or $208 million of this expansion, took place since 1945; that is, after the extraordinary expansions of the war. Perhaps still more surprising is the fact that two-thirds of the post-war expansion took place in the years 1950 and 1951 when the bank was supposed to be following a "definitely restrictive approach to the whole question of credit restriction".
That quotation, of course, ties in with what I have just said about the amendments to

the bill. Since this article was written- and it was written in May, 1953-the annual report of the Bank of Canada indicates a decrease in chartered bank reserves of $11-4 million in 1953. Thus only in two years since the war, namely in 1947 and 1953, have chartered bank reserves decreased; in other words their ability to issue credit and to make loans declined only in those two years.
In all the other years since the war the reserves of the chartered banks showed an increase and hence, in our opinion, inflation was promoted. Consequently the suggestions made in the bill with regard to bank reserves are very important. An examination of the production and monetary situation since the end of the war leads me to say that I think the government itself can be blamed for failure to promote a better balance between fiscal and monetary policies and production to combat inflation. This taken in conjunction with the removal of wartime controls explains the manner in which the costs of living have increased and gives valid reasons why both farmers and workers have been asking for better returns for their produce and their labour.
The main point I wish to make is that either because of insufficient control of the chartered banks, which we believe can only be effectively undertaken by public ownership of these institutions, or by failure of the government to use the central bank as effectively as it might have done, inflation got out of hand. I say that the committee should inquire into this matter, and I think the government and not the bank must assume responsibility for it.
I should like to summarize what I have in mind by a quotation from the monthly report of the Bank of Nova Scotia for the month of March, 1952. It reads as follows:
Judging by the experience of the past quarter century, there is no doubt that changes in the money supply are much more important than changes in the rate at which money is used. It is. therefore, clear that effective control of the money supply is of great importance in maintaining orderly economic conditions, and in combating inflation. From the standpoint of inflation, what matters is not so much the actual increase in the supply of currency and bank deposits but whether the supply of money is increasing more rapidly than the quantity of national production.
It seems to us that has been the case in the years between 1945 and 1953. Therefore we say, because the powers in the act which are now to be extended have not been used to the extent that they should have been, that Canadians have suffered from preventable inflation since the end of the war. I will not develop the thought I have in mind because, in view of what the Speaker said, it might be considered to be outside the scope
Bank of Canada Act
of the bill at the present time. But I would hope that some consideration will be given to the setting up of a national investment board. I believe there is a gap there. With the large funds accumulated by various financial institutions in the country, I believe that the time has come when we should endeavour, through an institution answerable to parliament, to direct the flow of such funds into fields that are socially desirable, into the development of our resources, into housing, into great projects like the South Saskatchewan river dam, the St. Lawrence seaway and so on which we need for the expansion of Canadian resources.
Therefore I hope that when the committee meets it will review the operations of the Bank of Canada very thoroughly and go into many other phases of the problem upon which I have not touched because I do not want to go outside the principle of the bill. I sincerely trust that a very thorough inquiry will be made and that we may get a report from the committee recommending further improvements in this very useful and, indeed, most essential of our Canadian financial institutions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks let me say that we consider the major proposals contained in the bill a definite step in the right direction. I refer to the amendments dealing with cash reserve requirements, and I am going to confine my remarks mainly to that matter. But on the other hand we feel that they are too restricted in degree to permit the government to institute what we consider to be a sound financial policy. By that I mean a policy that will encourage optimum development of our resources and permit the equitable distribution of the goods and services resulting from that development. I think most members would agree that during any long period of peace that has not been the case.
I want to say a few words with regard to the division of responsibility between the chartered banks, the Bank of Canada and the government with relation to the question of cash reserves. First of all, may I say that we in the Social Credit group are not critical of the chartered banks. I know that impression has got abroad, but we consider the chartered banks to be a highly efficient organization. On the other hand, we believe that they could give even greater service under a sound financial policy that would help to level out the booms and depressions from which we have suffered in the past. The chartered banks, in considering the question of whether or not they should expand their loans, have, I think, to consider three main points. First of all, they must

Bank of Canada Act
consider the creditworthiness of the borrower. I would say that is the main consideration. Then they must consider the effect that that expansion will have upon their cash reserves. The third point is the relationship between the amount of loans they make and the securities that they may hold-in other words, their position of liquidity.
I would say that it is not the responsibility of the chartered banks to decide whether or not the action of making additional loans will be an inflationary one. The question as to whether an over-all expansion of credit would be unduly inflationary is a matter for the Bank of Canada to decide in conjunction and in consultation with the government of the day. Then the Bank of Canada controls the expansion and contraction of credit by either expanding or contracting the cash reserves of the chartered banks. We are of the opinion that the amendments proposed in the bill will provide greater efficiency in controlling the cash reserves of the chartered banks. However, the actual responsibility for financial policy must rest with the government and not with the Bank of Canada.
I would certainly take issue with the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) on that point. I know that many people in this country will blame the Bank of Canada for financial policy instead of the government. I think that has perhaps arisen from the statement made some years ago by the then deputy governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Osborne. It will be recalled that some years ago Mr. Osborne stated that no self-respecting central bank would accept from the government a policy with which it did not agree. That matter was brought up in the House of Commons and the minister of finance of that day, Mr. Charles Dunning, pointed out that the statement did not really mean what it appeared to say. He said that all it meant was that if the policy of the government was one with which the Bank of Canada did not agree then the governor of the bank and his officials would resign, but the policy of the government would prevail.
While it is true that the government's financial policy has provided the money required to maintain a maximum war effort and has also operated quite satisfactorily in periods activated by the fear of war or in periods after war when the costs of war are still being met in the form of rehabilitation, reconversion and many other things, such is not the case during any prolonged period of peace.

Now, the Bank of Canada was set up in 1934 as a privately-owned institution. Then, when the Liberals came into power it was turned into a publicly-owned bank. I believe we were all pleased, at least in this party, when that change was made. The interesting point to note is that, in spite of the fact that the central bank was set up in 1934 and continued in operation from then on, we continued in a depression up until 1939. From 1936 to 1939 we repeatedly urged that the government borrow from the Bank of Canada in order to finance the various national projects, housing projects and others, not merely for the purpose of providing employment but for the purpose of providing the services that the people desired and that we were capable of providing.
It is interesting to note the objection that was taken at that time to that proposal. It was argued that borrowing from the Bank of Canada would be more inflationary than borrowing from the chartered banks, the argument being that when money was paid out by the Bank of Canada it would increase the cash reserves of the chartered banks which would enable them to expand their loans on the ratio of 10 to 1 for the increased cash reserves. We suggested that argument could be overcome by the adoption of what was known as the 100 per cent cash reserve system. Under it we would have amended the Bank Act to compel the chartered banks to maintain a 100 per cent cash reserve behind their demand deposit liabilities. In order to secure the necessary cash they would have been able either to sell securities to the Bank of Canada or to borrow against them.
The argument against that, as presented by the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada, was that it would be too hard upon the chartered banks because they would lose the revenue from the securities that were turned over. As was pointed out by Babson back in 1936, that would not be necessary. All that would be necessary would be for the Bank of Canada to make a loan at a nominal rate of interest against the securities turned over by the chartered banks, and in that way the 100 per cent cash reserve would be maintained without any loss of revenue on the part of the chartered bank by the securing of that cash against their securities.
We pointed out at that time that that was one means. We were never dogmatic on the subject. We pointed out there were many other ways the chartered banks could be prevented from expanding their loans as a result of utilizing the services of the Bank of

Canada. The simplest proposal that we made was merely that, when money was issued through the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks would be required to increase their cash reserves in order to take care of the amount of money that had been issued, thereby denying them the right to expand their loans on the basis of the increased cash reserve. It is for that reason we welcome this measure because it provides for action of that kind, so that in the future we can make the cash reserve requirement variable as the situation warrants.
It will be recalled that upon the outbreak of war in 1939 the government borrowed from the chartered banks about $200 million within three months, I think it was, and expanded the savings of the people. Then, we borrowed the savings of the people by floating bond issues. Then, we borrowed again from the chartered banks in order to expand the amount of money in circulation and still further expand the savings of the people. Then, we borrowed the savings of the people. We carried out that process during the war. The net result of those transactions was a very heavy increase in the debt of the country. I note that, according to the Canada Year Book for 1948-49 and 1952-53, the gross debt in 1939 was $3,700 million and increased to $18,900 million in 1946; then dropped to $17,250 million in 1952.
Perhaps it would be fairer to take the net debt, so I will give the net debt for the same years. In 1939 it was $3,152 million; in 1946, $13,421 million; and in 1952 dropped down to $11,185 million. The interest charges on the net debt were $114,800,000 in 1939; $338 million in 1946 and down to $314 million in 1952. Unfortunately, today interest rates are going up so the interest charge on that net debt will also be going up correspondingly. While it is true that the government did finance the war in a way that provided whatever money was needed to maintain the maximum war effort, it cannot be argued for one minute that we maintained a pay as you go policy. It will be recalled that at the start of this war it was the intention of the government to maintain a pay as you go policy to the greatest degree possible.
On several occasions during the war we urged that, to the extent that heavy taxation and heavy borrowing from the savings of the people failed to meet government expenditures and it became necessary to have expansion of credit, that expansion of credit should take place through the Bank of Canada instead of the chartered banks. Then again we argued that in order to prevent that having an inflationary effect as a result of action
Bank of Canada Act
by the chartered banks, we should increase the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks to the amount necessary to make it impossible for them to use this increased cash as a basis for the expansion of loans.
After the war the Canadian economy remained in what you might call high gear, mainly as a result of reconversion of plant and equipment and the large loans that were made to foreign nations as well as the fact that people were spending the savings that had been developed during the war as a result of the compulsory savings feature of government policy. But by 1950 the situation had become tight again. Then, the Korean war blew the government economic policy off the rocks once again, and the situation became fairly liquid. Today we appear to be right back in the situation in which we were in 1950. I notice that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated that the situation today is similar to the situation that existed in 1950. No doubt many people are now asking whether or not there is another war around the corner that will once again help to revive economic activity within this country. No doubt when the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) returns from his tour around the world he will be in a position to reassure the members of the house on this point.
It does seem to me that one thing is certain. If it looks as though we are now entering a prolonged period of peace the government will be forced to take action to maintain the development of the resources of this country, to provide employment, to provide markets, and to provide for loans at a low rate of interest for housing the people in the low income brackets. It is quite evident that financial corporations are not going to be able to make that money available. The next question then is, if that is going to be done, how will a program of that type be financed? In 1943 I participated in a broadcast with the governor of the Bank of Canada entitled "The Shape of Things to Come". The subject was post-war finance. During that broadcast I asked Mr. Graham Towers a question-and I quote it now because I think it has a very direct relationship to the situation we are in at the present time. This was my question:
After the war the need will be to encourage private spending. Heavy taxes and public borrowing will be contrary to the public welfare. Will the government finance all desirable public projects by credit expansion when necessary?
To this Mr. Towers replied:
In circumstances such as Mr. Quelch describes, I would say that there would be grounds for the government not meeting the entire cost of its program by taxing and drawing on public savings. The desire would be to encourage private spending and make government investment more of a residual item. If part of the necessary money had to come

Bank of Canada Act
from credit expansion-and the projects were sound and in the public interest-then I would say go ahead.
Mr. Speaker, I would say that is just about the type of situation we appear to be running into at the present time. Some people look at the reports of the chartered banks, read that there is $5 billion of savings deposits, and jump to the conclusion that there is a large amount of money available for investment. But as was mentioned the other day by the president of the bankers association, that is not money available for investment. It is money that has already been lent, and is represented by loans. And therefore at the present time, if the chartered banks desire to expand loans, steps would have to be taken to increase cash reserves to allow them to make an expansion of credit on the basis of the increased cash reserves.
I say we have that situation today, because we hear a lot about unemployment increasing and we hear a good deal about the accumulation of inventories and surpluses. We read that today in some cases industries are having to reduce their production by 50 per cent. Then, in addition, we read that there is a very heavy program of instalment buying. I read that this amounts to 30 per cent of all sales-and I do not know whether that is a correct figure. However, we do know that there is a very heavy program of buying on the instalment plan, which shows that people who desire to acquire those things available for sale have not the money with which to buy them and, hence, are buying on time.
I think most hon. members will agree that perhaps the most immediate problem which needs to be met is that of providing houses for people in the low income groups. This cannot be provided by money from the various financial institutions, such as life insurance and mortgage companies. It seems to us that the logical body to provide finances for the financing of projects of that kind-housing, irrigation and any other projects-would be the government, through the Bank of Canada. And if there is to be credit expansion, then we certainly believe that that credit expansion should take place through the government's borrowing from the Bank of Canada.
Now, the proposed amendment gives the Bank of Canada the power to alter the minimum cash ratio to be maintained by the chartered banks within the limit of 8 per cent and 12 per cent of deposit liabilities. That is, the minimum cash reserve requirement will be raised from 5 per cent to 8 per 
cent; and then the amount to be held as cash reserve by the chartered banks will be made variable at the discretion of the Bank of Canada. There will be no change made in cash reserve requirements in excess of one per cent in any one month.
Having in mind that at the present time, in round figures, the deposit liability of the chartered banks is in the neighbourhood of $9 billion, and their cash reserves are in the neighbourhood of $900 million, then we find this situation. The general practice of the chartered banks is to maintain a 10 per cent cash reserve, so even if we raise the cash reserve requirements of the chartered banks to the full 12 per cent, it would only allow the government to borrow approximately $180 million from the Bank of Canada, without expanding the cash reserves of the chartered banks above the 12 per cent level. If they did, then the chartered banks would be able to expand their loans to 10 times the amount of the excess cash over that reserve.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we feel that the 12 per cent figure should be raised to at least 16 per cent, as a start. Then, as time goes on, and if it becomes necessary to increase the cash reserve requirements beyond that figure, it could be done, in order to allow greater leeway in borrowing by the government from the Bank of Canada.
Furthermore, we are of the opinion that there is no justification for limiting to one year the period of repayment of loans by the Bank of Canada to the government. We feel that the limit should be removed entirely. However, I realize that perhaps the government has no intention whatsoever of borrowing from the Bank of Canada. It will no doubt say that the amendments being made in connection with cash reserves are not for that purpose. But on the other hand we are faced with a situation where money must be available at a low rate of interest for various projects such as those I have mentioned- housing, irrigation and many other projects which may be considered worth while-in order to provide employment for the large number of unemployed we have in this country and thereby raise their standard of living.
After all, this is the government's responsibility. We have suggested a means by which it might be done, with only slight modification of the amendments proposed in the bill. Our suggestion would provide means of directing money to depressed areas at a low rate of interest through the government making loans to municipalities. It is all very well to have power to expand the cash reserves of the chartered banks in order to provide a high

level of activity, on the general level; but it is high time we had the means by which we could actually direct money into a depressed area. It appears that we do not have the power to do that; we do not have the machinery.
The minister has pointed out that this bill is to be referred to the committee on banking and commerce. Therefore I shall leave anything further I have to say to a time when the bill is before that committee. So far as some of the other amendments are concerned, I do not consider them of very great importance. There is the matter of arranging for the Bank of Canada to take mortgages into their portfolio on short-term loans. But I think it is quite evident that, in so far as the chartered banks are concerned, they are not likely to make much use of that provision; because they hold somewhere near $2,500 million in dominion bonds. Therefore, why should they try to get short-term loans on mortgages when they can obtain satisfactory returns on some of the securities they already hold? And certainly, judging from the remarks we have already heard from the president of the bankers association, they do not consider that provision is going to amount to very much.
In closing, let me say that we are not at any time attempting to be dogmatic in suggesting what should be done. We are merely pointing out that we have a situation in which there are large numbers of unemployed, a situation where there is urgent need for national housing to satisfy the requirements of people in low income groups. The evidence has shown that those people in the low income groups can obtain housing only if the money is loaned at a low rate of interest. We feel the government would be the logical body to do this. After all, this is a question of governmental responsibility; and we will back the government in any measures they may take in order to solve that problem, whether or not such measures are in line with the proposals we advocate.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make only two brief observations about the bill. The first is in connection with the bank's right to buy gold in coin or in bullion form, as of course it has the right to buy silver in coin or bullion form or, of course, nickel and copper coins.
I want to mention this because should an open bullion market be established in Canada, nothing would preclude the Bank of Canada from entering that market and buying either bullion or coin on the open market, just as at the present time it buys securities of the Dominion of Canada and I presume of
Bank of Canada Act
other nations. I do not know whether it buys United States securities, but I would imagine that it would at times buy shortterm American securities. So if a bullion market were established it would not mean that bullion gold would be hoarded, because of this provision of the Bank of Canada Act.
I want to make one further observation on the question of the definition of foreign exchange. Acceptable foreign exchange to the bank can be boiled down to currency convertible on demand at a fixed price into exportable gold. That is the sole qualification of a convertible currency. Let us assume that even if Russian rubles were freely convertible into gold at a fixed rate they would be acceptable as foreign exchange under the meaning of this act.
I think that shows more clearly than perhaps anything I could say the importance of the restoration by Canada of gold as a medium of exchange, and the facilitation of all measures by which currencies can be brought within this definition of acceptable foreign exchange as soon as possible, that is, convertible at a fixed rate into exportable gold.
I think that shows that gold is the one common denominator which is acceptable as a medium of convertibility. I would, as I shall on another occasion, urge that all possible steps be taken to bring gold out of the national hoards where it is now and use it as a measure to facilitate convertibility of all currencies. Canada in this regard is in a unique position to take the lead.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MANAGEMENT, EXCHANGE, TO PERMIT SHORT TERM LOANS ON INSURED MORTGAGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been very interested in this measure and in the remarks of the minister. While in full support of the amendment, I wonder why the provision with regard to the reserves of the chartered banks is put within rather tight limits, and why it is not left to the discretion of the governor and the board of the Bank of Canada. I presume the reason for this measure has been the need for greater control over the purchasing power in the country.
I think this is the time and the suitable place to call the attention of the house to the rather remarkable history of the Bank of Canada during the years since the end of the war. As we all know, we experienced a period of rapid upward spiralling of prices and a spiralling of cost of living which caused considerable embarrassment to various governmental authorities. During that period, for a curious reason which I shall refer to later, the Bank of Canada, far from acting to curb that inflationary spiral, apparently acted in precisely a contrary manner, as is revealed by its own Bank of Canada statistical survey.

Bank of Canada Act
We find that in 1945 the gross national product of Canada amounted to $9,315 million and the total money supply to $5,905 million. In 1950, five years later and after we had gone through some of the worst inflationary periods of our history, we find curiously enough that the gross national product was $10,330 million and the total money supply $8,712 million. In the case of the gross national product there was an increase of 11 per cent, while in the case of the money supply there was an increase of over 50 per cent. I presume that must have been the result of open market operations on the part of the Bank of Canada.
The question arises as to why they followed that course during a time when inflation was giving governmental authorities many headaches. The only conclusion I can come to is that it was necessary to maintain the market value of dominion government bonds. Possibly that was a perfectly logical reason for that action on the part of the Bank of Canada, because the government had virtually promised the people during the war years that their investment in government bonds would be readily redeemable at par any time. Moreover, as the government was facing the necessity periodically of refinancing, it was necessary to maintain public confidence in government bonds.
Here was the problem the government faced, working through the Bank of Canada. It was impossible to do the two things at the same time, maintain the market value of dominion government bonds and decrease the cash reserves of the chartered banks and by that means decrease the total money supply of the country. The government chose to maintain the level of government bonds.
I suggest that that points to two things, one of which was mentioned by the leader of this group when he was speaking; that is, the necessity of the government of Canada ultimately controlling the entire banking system of the country. It points also to something else, and I have a particularly personal interest in this. It points to the fact that this all stems from the government's financing policies during the years of the war.
As I say, I have a personal interest in this matter because I recall that on one occasion I was attacked in this chamber by a member of the House of Commons-I was a member of another legislative body at the time-who urged the authorities to have me arrested because I had suggested that the government's method of financing the war was bound to lead to serious inflation and trouble after the war, that the method of financing

by over 50 per cent loans was merely piling up trouble for the future. We are meeting that trouble today.
I presume that the government is hoping to cope with this trouble by means of various fiscal and monetary measures about which we have been told on occasion. I would point out that we are now entering a policy of economic contraction-I doubt whether my right hon. friend the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) would object to that modest expression-and it will not be possible for the government, purely by fiscal means, purely by monetary means, purely by the operations of the Bank of Canada, to combat that contracting tendency in the economy. In order to initiate expansion there will have to be something similar in nature to the projects which were undertaken by the government of Canada during the war, and from which stemmed the credit expansions which at that time had to be pooled or dammed, shall we say, and which at the present time are causing the inflationary troubles which have been in existence for the past few years.
I would commend to the government their own economic and financial history in facing the problems we have to face, including the problem of housing the Canadian people; and I would suggest to them that they will require to use the same sort of powers and mechanisms which they used in order to launch Canada upon its program of production during the war years.
